messages.author: 7dd668eb41c5bfd9
messages.subject: Tips for speed improvement?
parts:
Hi all,

I have a relatively simple hierarchical model:

data{
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> J;
row_vector[2] X[N];
vector[N] y;
int site[N];
matrix[J, 6] U;
matrix[2, 2] R;
}
parameters{
vector[2] B[J];
real<lower=0> sd_y;
cov_matrix[2] tau_b;
matrix[6, 2] Gamma;
}
transformed parameters{
vector[N] yhat;

for(n in 1:N){
yhat[n] <- X[n]*B[site[n]];
}

}
model{
row_vector[2] Bhat[J];
matrix[2,2] L;
for(j in 1:J){
Bhat[j] <- (U[j]*Gamma);
}
L <- cholesky_decompose(tau_b);

y ~ normal(yhat, sd_y) ;
B ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Bhat, L);

// Priors
to_vector(Gamma) ~ normal(0, 1);
sd_y ~ uniform(0, 10);
tau_b ~ wishart(3, R);
}

This runs fairly slowly. Whats more, it always seems like one or two chains gets stuck and take an extremely long to complete sampling. I've tried the Cholesky factorization approach outlined in the manual, but that didn't result in a substantial improvement and still has the same problems with chains getting stuck.

Does anyone have any advice for speeding up the model in general and preventing the chains from getting stuck?

Thanks!
Nate

messages.author: 7dd668eb41c5bfd9
messages.subject: Re: Tips for speed improvement?
parts:
To give some more detail, I just rain the model with 1000 iterations (to try and keep it quick). Three chains finished sampling within 15-20 seconds, while a fourth chain took 904 seconds to sample completely. Rhat ranges between 1 - 5, and is particularly bad for the gamma parameters (ranging from ~ 1.5 - 4.5). While this is to be expected from such low number of samples, running more iterations can take me nearly all morning. However, there is a trade off. For these iterations, I specified my own initial values, which helps the chains converge quicker and require fewer iterations. 

If I don't specify initial values, the model finishes sampling faster (all four chains in ~ 10-20 seconds), but there is no convergence (Rhat > 200). If I increase the number of iterations to 10,000, some chains finish rapidly (~100 seconds) while others require more time than I am willing to permit (> 1 hour).

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Tips for speed improvement?
parts:
Hi, I can’t comment on the Cholesky stuff but I noitce a big red flag here:
sd_y ~ uniform(0, 10);
First, if you want to do this, you should put the constraint in the declaration, not in this way in the model.  Second, don’t do hard constraints unless that’s part of the structure of the model.  Instead, do something like sd_y ~ normal(0,5) or whatever.

Beyond this:  are your X’s roughly on unit scale (no predictor that are scaled like .001 or 1000)?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Tips for speed improvement?
parts:
What you want to do is look at the regression chapter in
the manual on how to parameterize covariance matrices.

If you insist on Wishart priors, we can't help much yet on
speed or robustness (though making ones that are defined for
Cholesky factors is on our to-do list). But if you are willing
to go with our preferred LKJ priors, it should be both
much faster and more stable.

As to R-hat, anything bigger than 1.05 is bad --- the differences
in scale outside of that aren't telling you much other than that
you're a long way from convergence.

If you vectorize, you don't need to explicitly Cholesky decompose.
That should happen automatically inside multi-normal.

- Bob
